title: Checkpoint 0: Magnus vs Stockfish (skill 0)
notes: Checkpoint after game 0, from the Italian Game: Magnus plays the yardstick, Stockfish at skill 0. Nothing is studied afterwards.

moves.thought: This is the Italian Game after 4...Nf6; I avoid 5.Nxe5 (loses a piece to Nxe5) and 5.O-O (allows 5...Nxe4 tricks), choosing instead to defend e4 solidly. 5.d3 enters the Giuoco Pianissimo, keeping a sound structure with plans of Bb3, Nbd2, Re1 and a slow central build-up.

I considered d4 and the tactical Nxe5 (which only leads to an even trade after 6...Nxe5 7.d4 Bxd4), but the simplest and safest plan in this Giuoco Pianissimo structure is to get the king to safety and the rook to the f-file. After O-O Black has no checks or captures that trouble me (6...Bxf2+ 7.Rxf2 simply wins a piece).

I want to grab the centre while my pieces are developed and castled; 7.d4 hits e5 and opens lines. If 7...exd4 8.cxd4 Nxe4?? loses a piece to 9.Re1 pinning on the e-file, and 7...Nxd4 8.cxd4 exd4 9.Nxd4 just leaves me a clean pawn up with a dominant centre.

Black's d4 pawn must be recaptured, and cxd4 gives me the ideal two-pawn centre (d4+e4) rather than trading pieces with Nxd4; if Black grabs with 8...Nxe4 then 9.d5 kicks the c6 knight with tempo and Re1/Qf3 ideas give me a strong initiative against the e4 knight and f7.

I checked 9.e5 first and rejected it: Black answers 9...dxc4 10.exf6 Qxf6, winning a pawn and hitting my d4 pawn. Instead I resolve the center tension with 9.exd5, after which Nxd5 lets me gain time with Re1+ and Nc3 against the exposed knight, keeping my pieces active.

Black's two knights hit my d5 pawn, which only Bc4 defends, so I need extra support; Qb3 does it tactically — after Nexd5 Bxd5 Nxd5, Qxd5 recaptures along the b3–d5 diagonal, winning a piece for a pawn, while Nf3 still guards d4 against Bxd4.

I checked that d4 is safe (Bb6 attacks it but Nf3 defends), so I can develop with tempo instead of defending. Re1 puts the rook on the open e-file against the knight on e7 and the king on e8, creating the threat Bxd5 Qxd5?? Rxe7+ followed by Qxd5 winning material, while keeping Black's king stuck in the centre.

The tempting 12.Rxe7 Qxe7 13.Bxd5 fails to equalise because of 13...Qe1+ 14.Kh2 Qxc1!, snatching my loose bishop since Ra1 is blocked by the knight on b1. So I first play Bd2, which develops, defends f4, and makes the Rxe7/Bxd5 combination a genuine threat (now ...Qe1+ Kh2 Qxd2 simply loses to Nxd2), while Black's d5-knight stays attacked twice and defended twice.

Black's 12...Bg4 attacks the knight that defends d4, so my isolated pawn is the hot spot; I need to reinforce it. Be3 is well-protected (f2, Re1, Qb3 cover the square) and after any capture there I recapture with the f-pawn or rook, keeping a solid d4–e3 center, while Rxe7 fails to Nxe7 and h3 allows Bxf3 leaving d4 loose.

My only undeveloped piece is the b1 knight, and Nbd2 both develops it and means that after ...Bxf3 I can recapture with the knight instead of wrecking my kingside pawns; if Black trades ...Nxe3 I answer fxe3, keeping the d4 pawn protected and opening the f-file. I checked the tactics: ...Nf4 loses a piece to Bxf4, and ...Bxd4 is always met by a recapture, so nothing hangs.

Black's bishop on g4 is my opponent's most active piece, so I want to question it immediately with h3, which either wins the bishop pair after Bxf3 Nxf3 or gains time if it retreats to h5/e6. I checked the tactics: Bxh3 gxh3 just gives Black two pawns for a piece, and d4 stays defended by both Be3 and Nf3, so nothing drops.

The knight on d5 is well defended by Be6, so Bxd5 only trades my strong bishop for little, and tactics like Bxh6 fail because Qd8 guards b6. Instead I centralise with Ne5, where the knight is protected by the d4-pawn, eyes c6/f7/g6 and prepares Bxd5 or Nxc6 ideas while keeping my pieces active before Black gets in a4.

Black's knight on e3 must be answered, and recapturing with the f-pawn is best: it keeps my strong bishop and knight battery aimed at f7, opens the f-file for Re1-f1, and the e3 pawn shields d4 so ...Bxc4 Nxc4 never allows ...Qxd4 or ...Bxd4 (and after ...Bxc4 Nxc4 the b6 bishop is hit twice). I checked 17.Nxf7 Rxf7 18.Bxe6 Rf6!, which just loses a piece for a pawn, so I avoid that.

I must recapture on c4, and recapturing with the d2 knight is best: it keeps my strong knight on e5, is doubly defended (Qb3 and Ne5), and attacks the undefended bishop on b6. Recapturing with the queen instead fails to 18...Bxd4 19.exd4 Qxd4+ picking up the d2 knight, whereas after Ndxc4 ...Bxd4 19.exd4 Qxd4+ 20.Kh1 leaves c4 safely guarded and me a piece up.

Black's bishop on b6 is attacked twice (Qb3 and Nc4) but defended only once by the queen on d8, so 19.Qxb6 Qxb6 20.Nxb6 wins a clean piece; if instead 19...Nxe3, then 20.Qxd8 Rxd8 21.Nxe3 leaves me a bishop for a pawn ahead. I checked the alternative 19.Nxf7 line, but it only nets a pawn, so the simple capture is best.

My knight on c4 is attacked by the knight on b6 and undefended, so I must deal with that; since I'm down material (queen for a bishop), I don't want to trade pieces with Nxb6, which would leave Black's queen dominant. Retreating to d3 keeps both knights, supports e5 and c5, and crucially covers b2 so Qb6 doesn't pick off that pawn, while e3 stays guarded by my rook on e1.

I'm down a queen for a bishop, so I need maximum activity rather than passive defence; Nc4-c5 is a safe outpost (Black's own knight on b6 blocks b7-b6) that immediately attacks the loose b7 pawn with ideas of Nxb7 hitting the queen. I checked that Nxa5 just loses a piece to Rxa5 and Nd6 drops to Qxd6, while e3 stays defended by my rook on e1 after any ...Nd5.

I'm down material after the queen trade, so I need active play and pawn grabs: 22.Nxb7 takes an undefended pawn while hitting the queen on d8 and the rook on a8. The tricky reply 22...Qb6 (double attack on both knights) fails to 23.Nxa5! since Nc4 and Ra1 cover a5 — 23...Rxa5 24.Nxa5 Qxa5 25.Rxa5 wins, and after other queen moves I can even snap off a5 with the b7 knight, keeping the c4 knight as its defender.

Black's queen on e7 was threatening Qxb7, so I had to save that knight; the e3 pawn is fine because Nc4 guards it alongside Re1, so ...Nxe3 just loses a piece. Among the retreats, Nc5 lands on a square protected by the d4 pawn and attacked by nothing (Nd8 drops to Rxd8, Nbxa5 to Rxa5, and Nbd6 could later be ground down by Rfd8+Qe7), and it keeps both knights coordinated so I can follow with e4 to kick the strong Nd5.

Black's immediate threat is Nxe3, since after Rxe3 Qxe3+ he wins a rook and pawn for the knight; the e3 pawn can't be defended a second time. Pushing e4 sidesteps that tactic entirely, keeps the pawn protected by Re1, gains space, and hits the knight on d5 with tempo (and if the knight drops back to b6, Nxb6 just wins it).

Black threatens Rxd4 (d4 is undefended) while e4 is already covered twice by Re1 and Nc5, so Rad1 shores up the d-pawn without weakening the e-file. After Rad1, Nxe4 just loses a piece (Nxe4! and Qxe4 Rxe4), and Rxd4 drops the rook, so my center holds and both knights stay active.

Black's rook just landed on d4 where nothing defends it — the queen on e7 doesn't cover d4 and the knight on f6 guards d5/e4 only, so I simply win a whole rook. If Black answers Nxe4 I take with Nxe4, and Qxe4 loses the queen to Rxe4.

My rook on d4 is attacked by Rd8 and undefended, so I must resolve the d-file; Rd7/Rd6/Rd5 all drop material and Nb3/Nd6 either abandon the e4 pawn or are under-defended (Nc5 cannot reach d6). After the forced 27.Rxd8+ Qxd8 I plan 28.Rd1, hitting the queen with tempo and covering d4 so the annoying Qd4+ double attack on my knights never comes, after which Nd6 plus Nc5 hold e4.

My rook on d8 is attacked by the queen (e7–d8 diagonal) and undefended, so it must move; Rxe8+ Qxe8 would cut my advantage from rook+knight-for-queen down to much less, so I keep the extra material instead. Rd5 loses to cxd5, Rd6/Rd7 drop to the queen, and Rd4 allows Qe5 forking rook and knight — Rd2 is completely safe, guards a2/b2 and the second rank, and supports a future Nd3 which would hit a queen landing on e5 or b4.

I'm in check on the c5–g1 diagonal, so I must block or move the king; king moves (Kf1/Kh1/Kh2) all drop the knight to Qxc4, and Rd4/Re3/Rf2 either lose a rook outright or abandon the knight. Ne3 blocks and the knight is defended by Re1, so Qxe3+ Rxe3 would just lose Black's queen, keeping my rooks-and-knight versus queen material edge.

I checked the tactical safety of each rook move: Rd4, Rd6 and Rd5 all drop material to the queen (Qxd4, Qxd6, or cxd5/Qxd5), and Rd7 runs into ...Nf6 hitting both the rook and my loose e4 pawn. Rc2 keeps the rook defended by the knight on e3 (so Qxc2 Nxc2 wins the queen for a rook), blocks the c-file against ...Qc1 ideas, and pressures the weak c6 pawn while I keep Rc4 available to shore up e4.

The c6 pawn is completely undefended (the knight on e8 and queen on e7 don't cover it), so Rxc6 grabs a free pawn. I checked Black's counterplay: 31...Qb4 hits b2 and e1, but 32.Rd1 keeps everything safe, and 31...Qe5 is met by 32.Rc4 defending e4 — in both cases I stay a pawn to the good with two rooks and a knight against the queen.

Black's Qh4 threatens Qxe1+ along the h4–e1 diagonal, since my king doesn't cover e1, so I must deal with that first. Doubling with Rcc1 defends the e1 rook (Qxe1+ Rxe1 wins the queen), keeps e4 guarded by Re1, and consolidates my rooks+knight advantage against queen+knight.

My e4 pawn was attacked twice (Qh4 and Nf6) but defended only once, so Nxe4 followed by Rxe4 Qxe4 would have cost me material; pushing e5 solves that while gaining a tempo by attacking the knight on f6 (and if Black ignores it with Qg3 or Qf2+, exf6 nets a piece since Qxf6 only regains a pawn). If Black tries Ne4 I meet it with Rc4 hitting the undefended knight, and e5 keeps my extra rook-vs-queen material edge rather than simplifying.

Black's knight on d7 hits my e5 pawn, and my Ne3 currently blocks Re1's defence of it, so I reroute the knight to c4 where it both guards e5 (together with Re1) and attacks the loose a5 pawn. On c4 the knight is protected by Rc1, so Qd4+ achieves nothing, and ...Nxe5 just loses material after Nxe5 since Qxe5 runs into Rxe5.

I first checked Re4 and Nxa5: Re4 just loses a rook to Qxe4, and Nxa5 lets the queen in with Qd4+ followed by Qxb2 and Qxa2, giving the pawn straight back. Rc2 solves everything in one move — it defends b2 and the Nc4, covers the second rank (stopping Qf2 ideas), keeps Re1 supporting the e5 pawn, and prepares Nxa5 next with everything guarded.
Only one legal move is available — my king must step out of check to h2, since the queen on e1 cannot be captured or blocked.

Black threatens Qxe5+ (check on the b8–h2 diagonal) and the e5 pawn can't be defended, so I play g3 to block that diagonal, shelter my king on h2 behind g3/h3, and keep rook and knight mutually safe. If Black tries Nf4 I simply take with gxf4 winning a knight, and after Qxe5 or Qe4 I can hold everything with Rc3.

I checked that e5 is defended by the knight on c4 and that 38.Rg2?? allows ...Nf3 mate (g1/h1 covered by the queen, g2 blocked), while 38.h4? loses to ...Nf3+ Kg2 Nxh4+ gxh4 Qe4+ forking rook and knight. Rc3 keeps the knight on c4 protected, guards g3, and most importantly controls f3 so ...Nf3+ simply drops the knight to Rxf3, while keeping ideas of Rc8+ activity.
Only one legal move is available — the king must step to h1 since it is in check on h2.

I'm down a queen for a rook, so I need the most forcing try: Re3 attacks the undefended knight on e4 and is itself protected by Nc4 (and Rc2/Rf3 would simply drop the rook to the queen). I checked that Black's Nxg3+ Kh2 Nf1+ Kh1 is no mate, so Re3 at least poses a question and keeps my pieces coordinated.

Black's knight threatens Nxg3+, which would be mate if my rook ever left the third rank, so Re3 must stay guarding g3; capturing with Rxe4 would just hand over rook for knight since f5 defends e4. Instead I grab a free pawn with Nxa5, keeping my rook on the third rank so Nxg3+ is answered by Rxg3, and I stay close on material.

My knight on e4 is protected by the queen on c2, so Rxe4 just loses the rook, and rook moves to e2/d3/c3/b3 all drop it to the queen. Rf3 is the one square where my rook is safe from both queen and knight while also guarding g3 and h3 (killing the Nxg3+ trick) and pressuring f5.

I'm down a queen for a rook, so my best practical chance is to force matters: Rf1 blocks the check while attacking the queen, and if Black grabs it with Qxf1+ Kxf1 I trade my rook for the queen and emerge two pawns up in a knight endgame. If Black declines with something like Qd5, I can return Rf3 to cover g3 against the Nxg3+ fork and aim for a repetition.

My rook on f1 was undefended and attacked by the queen, so I had to move it; Rxf5 fails to gxf5, Re1/Rd1 drop the rook to Qx, Kg1 loses to Qf2+ and Rf2/Rf3 are simply captured. Rf4 keeps the rook safe (not touched by Qe2, Ne4 or the pawns), attacks the knight on e4 and the f5 pawn, and meets Nxg3+ with Kh2 winning the knight.

Rf1 loses the rook outright to Qxf1+ since my king on h1 doesn't guard f1, so I must step aside. Between Kg2 and Kh2 I prefer Kg2: it shields the g3 pawn, covers f2 (stopping Nf2 tricks), and only allows Qe2+ where I can shuffle back for repetition.

Rf2 looks active since it attacks the queen, but the queen is defended by the knight and f2 is attacked twice (Ne4 and Qe2) while only defended by my king, so Nxf2! Kxf2 wins my rook for a knight and leaves me with a knight against a queen. Kh1 also loses material to the fork Nf2+, so I step to g1, where after Qe1+/Qe3+ I can oscillate with Kg2 and repeat the position.

Rf2 fails to Nxf2! since my king can't recapture (Qe3 guards f2), and Kh1 runs into Nf2+ followed by the deadly Nxh3+ double check hitting my rook, while Kh2 allows Nxg3 with my king exposed. Kg2 keeps the king on the safe square, repeats the position (which suits me since Black's queen is nominally stronger than my rook and knight), and if Qf2+ ever comes I simply answer Rxf2 winning the queen for the rook.

Rf2 looks like it traps the queen, but Nxf2! works because the queen on e2 guards f2, so I'd simply lose a rook for a knight in an already slightly worse material situation. Since Black is nominally better (queen vs rook+knight), I steer into the perpetual-check repetition: after Kg1 the position after move 46.Kg1 recurs, and 48...Qe3+ 49.Kg2 Qe2+ 50.Kg1 would be a threefold draw.

Black's knight on g3 means Qf1 would be mate if my rook ever leaves the f-file, so I must keep f1 covered; Rf2 does that while simultaneously attacking the queen with the rook protected by my king. If Black trades with Qxf2+ Kxf2, I reach a knight-and-pawns endgame a pawn up, and otherwise the queen must retreat while Rf1/Rf2 keeps repeating the attack.

Black was threatening 50...Qh1# (h1 is covered by the knight on g3 and my king has no flight square), so I had to address the long diagonal; Rg2 blocks it, is defended by my king, and simultaneously attacks the undefended knight on g3, so after e.g. Qxg2+ Kxg2 I even win the knight, and Nf1 or Nh1 just drops the piece.

Material is actually balanced (R+N+4P vs Q+3P), so I must avoid any trade of a piece for the queen or of knights, and instead shelter my king. Kh2 defends the rook on g2, adds a second attacker on the g3 knight, and leaves Black with only one check (Nf1+), after which Kh1 keeps everything guarded; Kf2 by contrast invites Qd4+/Qc2+/Ne2 tactics against my loose rook.

My rook on g2 is my lifeline (defended by the king, pinning the g3 knight against h4), so I avoid loose rook moves like Re2 (Qxe2) and Rd2/Rc2, and I reject Rxg3 hxg3+ Kxg3 since knight-and-pawns versus queen is hopeless. Nb3 is the only knight move that is protected (by a2 and b2) and it heads for d4, where it covers e2/f3 and supports pushing my passed e-pawn for counterplay.

I must not trade my rook for the knight (Rxg3 hxg3+ Kxg3 leaves me a queen down against a knight), so I need a safe, active rook square. Rf2 stays protected by my king, keeps b2 defended along the second rank, attacks f5, and takes away f1 and e2 so Nf1+ would simply lose the knight to Rxf1.

I'm in check from the queen on the e5–h2 diagonal after the discovered check, and Rf4 just loses the rook to Qxf4+ since nothing defends f4. Between the king moves, Kg2 invites ...Nf4+ followed by ...Qe3 skewering my pinned rook, whereas after Kh1 the checks (...Qe1+) can be answered by Kh2 keeping the rook defended, so I retreat to the corner.

All three king moves keep the rook on f2 protected or safe, but Kg2 is the most active: it attacks the loose knight on g3 (defended only by the h4 pawn) and takes away both Ne2 and Nf1, since Rf2 covers e2 and f1 while the king covers g3. Checks like Qe4+ or Qd5+ only chase my king to g1, where Ne2+ would simply lose the knight to Rxe2 if it comes unsupported.

I'm material down, so I need a consolidating move that loses nothing: Rf3 immediately fails to Qe2+ Kg1 Qf1+ Kh2 Qxf3, Rxf5 drops the rook to Qxf5, and Rf4/Re2 lose to gxf4 and Qxe2+. Nd2 brings the knight to a square protected by my rook, covers the key f1, f3 and e4 entry squares, and after Qe4+ I can safely block with Rf3 (defended twice).

The knight on e2 is defended by the queen, so Rxe2 Qxe2+ just loses the exchange; instead Nf3 is safe (defended by Rf2, and neither Qe5 nor Ne2 covers f3) while hitting the queen and both the g5 and h4 pawns with tempo. Trading off Black's pawns is my best practical hope of reaching a drawable R+N versus Q fortress, so I grab the initiative.

I checked whether my rook on f2 was actually attacked — the knight on e2 doesn't hit f2 and the queen's path along the second rank is blocked by its own knight, so there is no immediate threat and Rxe2 would just lose a rook for a knight since Qb2 covers e2. Instead I grab a pawn with Nxg5, which keeps my rook, removes a kingside attacker, and leaves my king shielded; Black's Nf4+ ideas can be met with Kf1 or Kg1.

I must move the king, and I noticed Kh1 or Kh2 would simply drop my rook (Qxf2), while Kf1 is mate after Qb1+ since my rook can't reach the first rank and e2/g2 are covered by the knight. Kf3 runs into Qb3+ with my king stripped of shelter, so Kg1 is the only move that keeps the rook defended and answers Qb1+ with the blocking Rf1.

Black's knight on f4 plus queen create immediate mating threats, so trading the rook for the knight is the only way to defuse the attack. After Rxf4 Qxf4 I get Ne6 hitting the queen with tempo, leaving queen versus knight and two pawns — bad, but far more defensible than allowing Qe1+ and the knight joining the mate.

My knight on g5 is attacked by the queen on f4, and most retreats lose it (Ne4 and Nf3 drop to Qxe4/Qxf3, Nh7 to Kxh7, Nf7+ to Kg8/Kg7 followed by capture). Ne6 is the one square that is neither covered by the queen nor the king, so I keep my only piece and fight on.

I'm down a queen for a knight, so my priority is to avoid immediate loss of material and stay compact around my king. Both a3 and a4 drop the pawn to the queen on b4 (Qxa3 / Qxa4), and Nd4, Nc5, Nf4 all lose the knight at once, so I chose Ng5, which keeps the knight safe, defends h3 and f3/e4 near my king, and pokes at f7.

I checked each king square for queen checks that simultaneously hit my loose knight on g5: Kh2 and Kf1 both allow Qf4+ forking the knight, and Kg2 allows Qg4+ doing the same. Only Kh1 leaves no checking square that also attacks g5 (Qg1+/Qg2+ would just be captured), so it keeps my knight for now.

I'm a queen down, so my only goal is to avoid immediate loss and keep my knight — blocking with Ne4 or Nf3 just drops the knight to Qxe4+/Qxf3+. Kh2 allows Qd2+, forking my king and the g5 knight, so I step to g1 where no such fork exists (Qd5 doesn't reach g5 because the f5 pawn blocks the rank).

Every king move runs into Qd2+, which checks along the second rank and simultaneously hits my knight on g5, so the knight is lost in all lines; Kh2 would also walk toward the corner where my lone king risks a quick mating net. I pick Kf2 to keep my king active and central, so after Qd2+ I can answer Kf3 or Kg1 and try to grab the f5/h4 pawns or seek a perpetual.

I'm down to king, knight and two pawns against queen and two pawns, so my only goal is to avoid immediate mate and keep the knight defended-ish; Kf3 walks into Qd3+ and a wandering exposed king, while Ke1/Ke2 invite Qd2/Qd3 nets. Kg2 keeps my king near the h3 pawn and the g5 knight with no forced loss next move, so I'll shuffle back there.

I'm in a lost ending (queen versus knight and two pawns), so my only practical aim is to dodge checks and look for repetition. Kf3 is unsafe because the king walks into the queen's crossfire near the f5 pawn, and Kg1 invites Qf2+ driving me into the corner anyway, so I step to h1 where after Qd1+/Qe1+ I can shuffle between h1 and g2 and hope for a threefold repetition.

Kh2 allows Qg3+ followed by Qxh3+, losing my h-pawn and exposing my king further; Kg2 keeps the king guarding h3 and only permits harmless checks like Qe2+ or Qe4+. So I play Kg2 to keep my pawn and stay solid.

I'm in check from the queen on g3 (which is protected by the h4 pawn, so Kxg3 is illegal) and only Kf1 or Kh1 are available; my g5 knight is already attacked along the g-file and falls either way. I pick Kf1 because retreating to the h1 corner invites the standard Qg2/Qh2 mating nets with Black's h4 and f5 pawns supporting, while from f1 my king keeps the f1-g1-f2 shuffle squares and stays out of the corner.

I'm in check from Qd3 and must move the king; I checked every square and Black can always win the loose knight with a check (Qe3+ after Ke1/Kg1, Qf4+ or Qd2+ after Kf2, Qg3+ after Kg2), so I pick the move giving my king the most escape squares and no mate threats. Kg2 keeps the king off the edge, covers f1/f2/f3/g1/h1/h2 flight squares, and there is no mate in one.

I'm a queen down and just need to stay out of mating nets while my knight generates checks (Nf7+ ideas), so I only have to compare the two king retreats. On h1 my king is cramped against my own h3 pawn and Black's h4 pawn, where ...f4-f3 followed by Qg2 is a real mating net, so I prefer Kg1 which keeps f1/f2/h2 flight squares and no immediate mate (Qf2+ would simply be Kxf2).

I'm in check from Qe3 and only king moves are legal; unfortunately Qe3 also hits my knight on g5, which nothing defends, so it will fall whichever way I step. Between the options, Kg2 keeps my king off the back rank/corner where mating nets appear fastest and invites another Qe2+ shuffle that could head toward a repetition.

I must step out of check and the material situation is hopeless, so I want the king square with the most escape routes and no quick mating net. Kh1/Kh2 invite ...Qg3+ and the h-file/h4-pawn mating pattern, while Kf3 is too exposed to ...Qg3+ and the advancing f-pawn, so I chose Kf2, which keeps e1, e2, e3, f1, f3, g1 and g2 available.

Only two legal moves since I must escape the check on the g3 queen; Kf1 drives my king toward the corner where Black's queen mates quickly, so I prefer Ke2, running toward the centre and queenside where my king stays closer to the a2 pawn and further from Black's f5/h4 pawns. The material situation is hopeless, so I just aim to maximise resistance and hope for a stalemate or perpetual-check resource.

My h3 pawn is already attacked by the queen on g3 and can't be saved, so I should get my king active and away from checks rather than play Kf1 (allowing Qxh3+ with tempo) or waste time on a-pawn moves while the king sits exposed. Kd2 walks the king toward the queenside where Black's f- and h-pawns are far away, and I can still try to run my a-pawn.

I'm down to a bare king with two pawns against a queen, so I just need the most active square; d3 is not attacked by the queen and lets my king head for e4 to pressure the f4 pawn, unlike the passive Kd1/Ke1.

I'm down a queen for two pawns and simply lost, so I'm playing for maximum practical resistance: I keep my king close to my only passer and away from the black king and pawns. Ke4 steps toward the enemy pawns and allows immediate checks that drive me back, so I choose Kc3, staying compact next to the a-pawn and preparing a2-a4.

I'm lost material-wise (queen vs two pawns), so I just need the king move that keeps my a2 pawn protected and avoids being boxed in. Kb2 keeps the king compact next to a2, and after checks like Qd4+ or Qb5+ I can still shuffle, whereas Kd3/Kd2 drift away from the pawn and invite more awkward checks.

I must escape the check, and the one real danger is my king landing on a1 where (with my own pawn on a2 blocking) Black mates with Qc1#, so I rule out Ka1. Black's king is far away on h8, so the lone queen cannot force mate quickly if my king stays in the open, so I head toward the centre with Kc3, where no check wins material (Qb4+ would simply be met by Kxb4).

I'm lost material-wise, so my priority is avoiding a quick mate: staying near the a1 corner with my own a2 pawn risks patterns like Ka1/pawn a2 with Qb3#, so I steer the king away from the corner. Kd3 keeps the king central with flight squares (after Qd6+ I have Kc3, Kc2, Ke2, Ke4) and heads toward Black's advanced f- and h-pawns.

I'm a lone king with two pawns against a queen, so my only hope is to avoid mate and stay away from the edges where a mating net can form, while keeping an eye on Black's f4/h4 pawns. Ke4 is not attacked by the queen (d6 covers e5/f4 and c5, not e4), keeps my king maximally central, and Qd4 would just be captured; Black's king on h8 is far too distant to help force mate soon.

Down to a queen versus two pawns, my only practical chance is activity, so I step to f3 where my king attacks the f4 pawn and stays away from the back-rank/edge mating nets near Black's king. If Black checks with Qb3+, I simply reply Kxf4, and f4 is only held as long as the queen stays passive on the fourth rank.

The f4 pawn is undefended — Black's queen on c3 can't reach f4 (the rank-3 line is blocked by my own king and the c3-h8 diagonal misses f4), so Kxf4 wins a free pawn and reduces Black's attacking material. The alternatives like Kg4 leave the pawn alive and allow Qg3+ ideas, so capturing is clearly best.

I'm lost on material, so my only practical hope is to eliminate Black's last pawn; Kg5 is not attacked by the queen (which covers g4 and f5 but not g5) and threatens Kxh4. If Black answers Qg3+ I can step to f5 or f4 and keep harassing the h-pawn, whereas Ke4/Ke5/a-pawn moves let Black queen the h-pawn quickly.
